column2: “Have you eaten?” “Yes,” A’qiao replied. “I've been wanting some of Lugaojian's pork in soy sauce for ages. Today I finally had it.” As she helped him undress and wash his feet, she asked what had happened at He Guiqing's. Hu could hardly tell her about going to the capital to seek a transfer, and apart from that there was little to say. He had not seen a single member of He's family. Once they were in bed, she asked from her pillow, “What about tomorrow? Where would you like to go?” “The business is finished. Where shall we spend the day? I can't come all the way to Suzhou and say I haven't even seen Tiger Hill.” This surprised her. “I thought your business would take several days. In that case...” “What is it?” Her hesitation surprised him in turn. “I'd meant to go home to Mudu. Now it seems I can't.” “That needn't matter. What do you want to do there?” “What an odd question! My home's in Mudu. How could I come to Suzhou and not go back?” “Oh!” Hu blurted out. “You're going to see your husband?” “Must you put it so unpleasantly?” She was flustered and angry. “I'm going to my parents' home.”

From her expression, she appeared to be telling the truth. Hu felt he might as well ask further. “Who's left in your family?” “My mother and a brother. I'll see them, take them a little money and come straight back to the city.” “How long would that take?” “Two days for the journey there and back.” “Two days?” He considered. “Go tomorrow, then, and return the day after. We'll leave as soon as you're back.” “Then I shan't be able to go to Tiger Hill with you tomorrow,” she said apologetically. “That doesn't matter. A’qiao, what exactly is the arrangement between you and your husband's family?” “What arrangement? So long as I give them money, they don't care about anything.” Her tone was contemptuous. “Do you send money every month?” “Sometimes every month, sometimes every two months. More when I have more, less when I have less. There's no fixed rule. It also depends on finding someone going that way. Always having to ask people is a real nuisance.” “Wouldn't it be better to make a clean break? That would save you the trouble.” She said nothing and seemed troubled. Hu wondered what the difficulty was. “A clean break is possible. I'm afraid they'll demand an outrageous sum.” “How outrageous? Country people can hardly ask for very much.” “It would take at least two thousand taels.”

Two thousand was indeed an outrageous demand. Even marrying a celebrated courtesan from a changsan house in Shanghai would cost no more. Fine woman though A’qiao was, her value in such a transaction did not amount to that. If he simply said, “Then two thousand it shall be,” he would not win a reputation for generosity. He would look like what the foreign settlement's new slang called a gullible customer. Of course, he felt this way because his interest in her had diminished since she involuntarily betrayed her feelings for “Mr He.” Otherwise, the thought of being made a fool of would not have arisen. “We'll discuss it when we get back to Shanghai,” he answered coolly. “I haven't that much money with me.” In fact, he carried three thousand taels in banknotes. It was an excuse. A’qiao had expected no such offer, however, and was not disappointed. The night passed without further incident. In the morning, Hu kept his promise of the night before and urged her to go to Mudu. “I feel bad leaving you alone at the inn. Why don't you come with me?” What sort of arrangement would that be? Country customs were restrictive. Even if she did not mind bringing a lover home, Hu would feel embarrassed. He waved the suggestion aside. “Never mind. Go on your own. I shall enjoy looking round the city by myself.” “Then I'll set out early tomorrow morning. I should be back about noon.” She asked Jinchang Inn to hire a sedan chair for the return journey. Hu felt it would be rather shabby to let her go empty-handed without making any gesture himself. He took out a hundred-tael note, saying it was for her parents to buy nourishing medicines. Naturally delighted, she seemed still more reluctant to part when she got into the chair.

She had scarcely left when He Guiqing sent another invitation, this time to lunch at the Lion Grove Garden. Hu had been wondering where to go and gladly accepted. He sent back a reply, tipped the messenger and took a sedan chair through Chang Gate. After drinking a bowl of tea at Xuanmiao Temple and buying a few small jade objects at the temple market, he hired another small chair outside the temple shortly before noon and went to keep the appointment. The Lion Grove was famous for its rockery, said to have been designed by Ni Yunlin himself. Its paths twisted, rose and fell in strange, unpredictable ways. He personally conducted Hu through it, pointing out its features with the utmost attentiveness. A circuit took about an hour and left them tired enough to find the food especially good. Only after they had eaten a fair amount did conversation become lively. Official affairs were unsuitable for such an occasion, and He knew nothing of commerce, so they talked of scenery and romantic pleasures. With a little wine in him, He grew more expansive and less guarded. When they reached the subject of family, he suddenly said, “Brother Xueyan, there's something I must ask, though I'm embarrassed to do so. My wife is frail and often ill, and she has the most generous disposition. She frequently urges me to take a concubine who could share her burdens and attend to my meals and daily needs. I do see the necessity. But as an official serving in Jiangsu, I am strictly forbidden to take a woman under my jurisdiction as a concubine. On this journey to the capital, I shall need someone close to look after me. Could you find a suitable woman for me in Shanghai or Hangzhou?” “Nothing could be easier. Tell me what sort of woman you like.” “Someone like A’qiao would be ideal,” He answered without thinking.

Hu started. Studying He's expression, he concluded that this did not seem to be a disguised request for A’qiao herself, and felt somewhat better. “I understand,” he said, nodding. “Before you leave, I shall certainly have something to report.” “Thank you! I'll send five hundred taels over presently. Please arrange it within that sum.” “It won't cost so much. Nor need you send the money. Once it's settled, we'll reckon everything together. I'll even ask for a reward.” “You put it too strongly. I ought to thank my matchmaker.” Hu had agreed, but back at Jinchang Inn he realized that finding another woman like A’qiao would be no easy matter. “Ah! How foolish I've been!” Breaking through the obstruction in his mind, he solved the difficulty, only to be left with a sense of loss. Why seek someone like A’qiao when A’qiao herself was already there? Yet letting her go felt different from giving up A’zhu. When he had redirected the match, joining A’zhu's red thread of marriage to Chen Shilong's, his conscience had been clear and he had felt positively pleased. Now, at the thought of sending A’qiao into another man's arms, his heart was sour with unhappiness. He paced back and forth, turning the matter over repeatedly. Was there no better way?

His thoughts went round and round like an ant circling a millstone until it was almost dark. Then someone called from outside, “Mr Hu!” The voice was familiar, though for a moment he could not place it. Going out, he dimly made out Zhou Yiming. “When I called at noon, you were out?” “Oh, I'm sorry to have missed you. Education Commissioner He invited me to the Lion Grove.” “And the young mistress is away too?” “She's gone home to Mudu. She isn't my concubine, by the way. There's no need to call her that.” This was something of a rebuff. Zhou could find no answer and said, merely to fill the silence, “Why haven't you lit a lamp?” “Ah!” Only now did Hu notice. Amused at himself, he gave half the truth. “I've been so absorbed in something on my mind that I forgot. Old Zhou, let's go for a drink.” “Certainly.” Zhou smiled ingratiatingly. “I'd been hoping to act as host and offer you a cup, but I was afraid you wouldn't honour me and didn't dare suggest it.” “Nonsense! Why wouldn't I? You're far too polite.” Hu liked him and wanted to talk, so he added earnestly, “I'll be your guest. But I won't go to a restaurant. It isn't that I'm afraid of making you spend too much. First, I've had too much rich food at lunch. Second, I'd like to see what Suzhou's little taverns are like and how they differ from Hangzhou's.” “Then I'll do as you say. There are plenty of places devoted to drinking in front of Xuanmiao Temple. They're clean, and we could sit awhile.” “Good. Let's go.”

Hu slipped on an outer jacket, told an inn servant to lock his door and hired a carriage with Zhou to go into the city. The area before Xuanmiao Temple blazed with lights and bustled with people. Since Jiangning had fallen, Suzhou had become the province's foremost city. Several hundred civil and military officials had appeared almost overnight. Most had not brought their families and had nowhere to go when work was done. They congregated here, some strolling, others drinking themselves tipsy, and the market remained busy until the second watch. Every tavern was full. At last they found seats facing the street in one called Yuandachang. They sat down and ordered Shaoxing huadiao. Two or three older women, neatly and cleanly dressed in blue cotton, promptly approached with baskets of braised snacks to accompany the wine. The duck heads and wings looked good enough, though their flavour was unremarkable. But Hu had come to savour the atmosphere of a Suzhou tavern, not its food, and did not much mind. Once settled, after their first round of wine, he looked about him and began to observe. Suzhou natives were easily recognized by their composed manners, courteous deference and scholarly air. The two men at the next table were examples: both white-bearded, both speaking the local dialect in wonderfully soft voices. Merely listening to their animated conversation was a pleasure. War blazed on every side, yet Yuandachang was full of warm wine, gentle voices and leisurely enjoyment. The two old men were recalling the Jiaqing years, discussing inkstones, Yixing Gongchun teapots and bamboo carvings—the elegant playthings of scholars in a peaceful, prosperous age.

“What is a man alive for?” Hu asked, suddenly moved. “Simply to eat and drink his way through life?” Zhou stared blankly. He could not answer; he could scarcely even understand the question. “I mean people like those two old gentlemen,” Hu explained, lowering his voice. “They're probably country gentry living on rents. We have plenty of such families in Hangzhou. An ancestor held office and acquired some land. Unless a spendthrift appears, quiet living leaves enough to feed a generation or two. The men themselves generally have some examination standing. The better ones are licentiates admitted to the schools; otherwise they've paid twenty or thirty taels for the status of an Imperial Academy student. They count as people of standing too. All year round they're busy doing nothing: they sit in teahouses by day and have a bowl of wine at night. They drift pleasantly on until sixty or seventy, then stop breathing and go home to meet the King of Hell. ‘I've had my turn in the world of the living,’ they say. Ask what they did there, and the answer is nothing! Even being a ghost would be meaningless for someone like that.” Whether he was mocking himself or teasing others was unclear, but Zhou understood this much. He too had ambitions and felt considerable sympathy. “Quite so. A man should accomplish something in his lifetime, if only to do right by his parents.”

At that, Hu felt they could talk. “Old Zhou, I hear you were quite a figure in the navy.” “I wouldn't say I had a name, but I got on well with people.” Zhou took a drink and poured out his grievance. “Boatmen used to call me ‘Officer’ and treat me with great respect. Now it's ‘Old Zhou’, and I have to run every kind of errand. It leaves a bitter taste.” “You'd like to return to the navy, then?” “Wishing won't help.” He shook his head. “My old commanding officer has risen higher still. He listened to that damned brother-in-law of his and hates me like poison. The only way to get back on the rolls would be to change my name and start again as a common soldier. How long would it take to get anywhere? I can only give it up.” “If you really want to go back, I could help. A naval commander can hardly be so very high an official. What if I asked Education Commissioner He to write a letter for you?” “With a letter from him, I wouldn't have to return to my old place. He and Governor Xu of Jiangsu passed the metropolitan examination in the same year. I could enter the troops under the governor's direct command. That would be far better than my old post.” “Very well. I don't know much about these things. Tomorrow I'll take you to see the commissioner, and you can tell him yourself.” Remembering how courteously He had treated Hu, Zhou concluded that they must be close friends and that success was assured. He was intensely excited, thanked Hu repeatedly and became still more attentive as host.

When Hu had reached a comfortable degree of tipsiness, he wanted no more wine. They ordered two bowls of noodles with a double topping between them: one came with pork braised until meltingly tender, the other with smoked fish. By exchanging toppings, they each had fish and meat. They ate and drank to their hearts' content for less than half a tael. Hu was thoroughly pleased. “It isn't how much money you have, but how you use it. I've seldom enjoyed a meal as much as this.” “That's because you knew I was treating you and expected nothing fine. You'd prepared yourself, so it seems good.” “That's what they mean by ‘contentment brings lasting happiness’. If you can step back a little in your thinking, there's nothing to trouble you.” That night, he approached the question of letting A’qiao go in this same spirit. Suppose he had never met her. Suppose she had died. Suppose some powerful patron had taken her from him. Each such reflection loosened his attachment a little. At last he made up his mind. “A gentleman helps others attain their happiness,” he told himself. Then he sighed, pulled the quilt over his head and went to sleep.

When he rose early the next morning, Zhou was already waiting. Acting as a temporary servant, he ran about attending to Hu's needs, so that even without A’qiao Hu felt no inconvenience. He had always preferred travelling without a servant for the sake of freedom and efficiency. But a man like Zhou might be useful to have beside him. On his return, whether in Hangzhou or Shanghai, he ought to look carefully for someone suitable. After Hu had washed, Zhou invited him into the city for morning tea. Understanding what was on his mind, Hu readily agreed. “Yes, yes. Afterwards, I'll take you to the commissioner and ask him in person for a letter.” They went to the Wuyuan teahouse. Suzhou teahouses differed from Hangzhou's. In Hangzhou, most had open halls and treated everyone alike. Gentry, pedlars and labourers were all customers once seated. In Suzhou, the different classes were separated and did not mingle. Hu enjoyed a crowd, so he and Zhou sat in the outermost hall, drinking tea and sampling the various pastries until ten. Judging the time right, they paid and strolled to the prefectural school to see He Guiqing. Out of regard for Hu, He treated Zhou courteously too, repeatedly asking him to sit. Zhou observed official etiquette, standing respectfully with his hands at his sides. At last he could not refuse and perched on the edge of a chair as though squatting. Hu felt sorry for his discomfort and explained their purpose briefly. “Governor Xu has gone to Shanghai to direct the troops in person,” He replied. Then he turned to Hu. “There is a good opening at present, though. It's tax collection. I wonder whether Mr Zhou would consider it beneath him.” “You flatter him. At which tax station?” “You've heard of the new levy called lijin?” “I've heard of it, but I don't yet know exactly how it works.”

“It was devised by a remarkable man from your own Zhejiang. Indeed, he comes from Xuexuan's jurisdiction: Changxing County in Huzhou Prefecture. His name is Qian Jiang.” Qian Jiang, courtesy name Dongping, was an Imperial Academy student from Changxing. Fond of bold talk and ingenious schemes, he resembled the wandering strategists of the Warring States. When the Opium War began, Yijing, an imperial clansman who was assistant grand secretary and president of the Board of Civil Appointments, received orders to direct military affairs in Zhejiang as General Who Spreads Awe. Qian presented himself at his headquarters with a plan: recruit brave men, surprise the British and capture their leaders. Timid Yijing dared not attempt such an extraordinary scheme and politely declined. Later, Lin Zexu fell into disgrace and was sent into exile. Qian, having advocated resistance to the British in Guangzhou, was likewise sentenced to military exile in Ili. They met there, and Lin greatly admired him. When Lin was pardoned and allowed to return within the passes, he arranged to clear Qian's conviction and brought him back. In the capital, Lin praised him among the high officials, and his reputation rapidly grew. Unfortunately, Lin died not long afterwards, leaving Qian without support. He then travelled with his schemes through the country between the Yangtze and Huai rivers. In Yangzhou, he met Lei Yixian and proposed two measures. The first was to obtain blank certificates for purchased ranks in advance, to be filled in and issued on the spot. The second was to introduce lijin.

The poor long to be rich, and the rich to be honoured: that is human nature. Merchants who had made fortunes, particularly the salt merchants of the Two Huai districts, were therefore especially fond of purchasing official rank. Even after contributing enough to become third-rank circuit intendants, they felt a blue finial insufficiently imposing. They were always seeking opportunities—funding military supplies, for instance, or contributing to river works—to spend large sums on a special recommendation. Only a second-rank red finial would satisfy them. Yet buying rank involved complicated procedures. Clerks at the Board of Civil Appointments had endless tricks. A man might remit his payment and still wait a year or two for the board's certificate establishing his rank. Naturally, this diminished enthusiasm. Qian's scheme catered precisely to wealthy merchants eager to taste official distinction: money in one hand, goods in the other. As soon as payment was made, the certificate would be completed and issued. Nothing could be more straightforward. Lei thought the proposal excellent and had Qian submit a memorial setting it out in detail. Since the scheme would deprive the board's clerks of their profits, the board initially rejected it. But the treasury was empty. The more than ten million taels accumulated under Qianlong and Jiaqing had been exhausted since the Opium War in the Daoguang reign by imperial commissioners commanding armies—Yijing, Qiying, Qishan, Saishang’a and others. Now, in confronting the uprising of Hong and Yang, the court wanted a good horse without having to feed it. If it forbade the horse even to find its own fodder, how could that be justified? Qian's ingenious proposal was therefore approved at last. Large quantities of blank certificates arrived from the board. Transactions were immediate and required none of the endless incidental fees. Quicker and cheaper, the new arrangement naturally drew crowds of buyers. With this revenue, Lei recruited local volunteers and was able to hold the Yangzhou–Zhenjiang area. But each sale of rank brought payment only once. A continuing stream required another source. Hence lijin.

Previously, the Qing had imposed only customs duties on travelling merchants. Its principal tax revenue came from the land and poll levy, but so much territory had been lost that receipts had fallen sharply. War had also depressed sales in the Two Huai salt market and reduced its tax yield. Lijin was to make up the shortfall: one li collected on every qian. The rate appeared slight, but small sums accumulated into a considerable amount. Lei first tried it at canal wharves such as Xiannümiao and Shaobo near Yangzhou. The results were good. The court then formally ordered Yiliang, Governor-General of Liangjiang, Xu Naizhao, Governor of Jiangsu, and Yang Yizeng, Director-General of Grain Transport, to introduce contributions of lijin for military funds in various places north and south of the Yangtze. After hearing He's account, Hu greatly admired Qian and longed to meet him. That was impossible for the moment, however, so he set the thought aside and returned to Zhou's prospects. “He served in the navy and knows people at wharves all along the canal and the Yangtze. If you give him this opportunity, he certainly won't neglect his duties or let you down.” “I know. Mr Zhou looks very capable, and with your recommendation I'm sure your confidence is justified. I'll write at once. Please sit awhile.” He withdrew to his study and wrote the letter himself. Though not yet a provincial ruler, he already had all the manner of a governor or governor-general. His characters, as large as walnuts, filled two sheets of eight-line letter paper. In keeping with the order of their examination success, he addressed Lei as his senior. Hu received the letter and thanked He for Zhou, who himself expressed his gratitude by kowtowing.

“Go back first,” Hu told Zhou. “I'll stay and talk with His Excellency.” Once Zhou had left, He told Hu that Xu Naizhao might be transferred from the governorship of Jiangsu. “A confidential letter from the capital arrived early this morning. I think I shall wait and see.” Why should Xu's transfer make him wait? After a moment, Hu understood: He must have a chance of succeeding him and wanted to observe developments. This change of plan would be decidedly unfavourable to Hu's side. He wanted to urge He to keep to the original course: first arrange a transfer as granary vice-minister, then seek appointment as governor of Zhejiang. That would make everything convenient for Wang Youling, Ji Heling and Hu himself, with helpful connections on every side. But he could not openly argue against something he had only guessed. If the guess was wrong, he would be shooting at no target and make himself ridiculous in He's eyes. Besides, Hu knew that hints and indirect approaches worked better than plain statements. After a little thought, he found his line of argument. “The governorship of Jiangsu used to be the finest post in the empire,” he suddenly remarked. “Now I should call it the very worst.” He naturally paid attention. “It's true that the post is no longer what it was, but hardly that it has fallen to the bottom.” “I'm only talking at random and seeking your advice.” Speaking slowly, Hu thought of reasons one at a time and offered them as they came. “First, the worst disorder is in Jiangsu. Less territory means less tax revenue.”

“Not so bad. We still hold the fertile Suzhou–Songjiang country.” Hu could hardly say that even Suzhou and Songjiang might be lost. “Holding it is hard enough. Liu Lichuan is still in Shanghai. But leave that aside. Second, Jiangsu has too many officials. The advantage of Zhejiang is that the governor stands supreme.” “Ah!” He nodded deeply. “There's sense in that. A governor and governor-general in the same city are indeed troublesome. Either the east wind overcomes the west or the west overcomes the east.” “It can hardly be easy for a governor to overcome a governor-general. But leave that aside too. Third, I've heard that General Xiang at the Jiangnan Grand Camp is difficult to serve. Is that true?” Of course it was. He reflected that the camp was full of arrogant troops and unruly commanders; Xiang Rong's difficult temper was the least of it. His intention of waiting in Jiangsu for a chance to succeed Xu began to waver. Seeing him silent, Hu guessed what he was thinking and pressed him with a further warning. “A local official must live or die with his city. Speaking privately on behalf of Governor Xu, my fellow native of Hangzhou, if he could be transferred elsewhere, it might truly be a case of the frontier old man's lost horse proving a blessing in disguise.” This struck home. He was extremely timid. However boldly he discussed warfare on paper, he was terrified of actual fighting. Jiangsu did seem to have become the worst of posts. Why seek trouble? Better go to the capital after all. Having decided, he could not say so openly. He merely nodded repeatedly. “Your argument is entirely right. I admire your insight.”

“What do I know? But as the saying goes, a bystander sees clearly. Without holding the post or having a personal stake in its gains and losses, one can see more plainly.” “Quite true. I need more guidance from men like you.” “You flatter me so much that you make me blush.” Hu took the opportunity to rise. “I must leave now, and take my leave of you before my journey as well.” “What?” He looked disappointed at once. “Are you going already?” “Yes. I mean to return to Shanghai early tomorrow.” “Then...” He considered for a long while. “We'll meet in Shanghai. It won't be very long.” “Certainly. As soon as I'm back, I'll have the money ready and wait for your instructions.” “There is also that other matter. I must ask you, whatever happens, to give it your attention.” Hu was momentarily puzzled, then understood. In fact, half the work was already done, and he could answer confidently. “Don't worry. Once I reach Shanghai, I shall have good news.” He was naturally delighted, and his excessive pleasure turned reflective. “To think that this visit should unexpectedly have made such close friends of us! Life is all a matter of affinity. It's truly beyond understanding.” Hu's circumstances resembled his in some degree. With Wang Youling, they were three men from distant corners of the country, brought together by some unseen force. Like the pieces of a tangram, apparently unrelated, they had combined into a pattern. It was wonderfully ingenious, and Hu felt deep sympathy with He's words. “Speaking of affinity, there's something else that will surprise you. I won't reveal it yet; that would spoil the pleasure. I only hope you'll reach Shanghai before the festival if possible, and shortly after if not. Then we'll talk again.” Hearing this, He would not press. “Very well. We'll talk then. Our next meeting is not far off, so I won't see you off on your journey.” “You needn't trouble yourself. Nor shall I call again to take leave.” Hu rose and bowed.

“Wait a moment.” He hurried back into his study and did not reappear for some time. He was writing on visiting cards himself. There was no time for letters, so he used seven or eight cards, one for each of the civil and military officials controlling the districts along the route from Suzhou to Shanghai. Ostensibly, they conveyed his regards; in reality, they introduced Hu. “Keep these in reserve,” he said, handing over the little stack. “The wording will tell you how close I am to each man. Judge for yourself which to use, whether to use them and how.” “These cards are as good as sending a hundred soldiers to protect me. I can sleep all the way to Shanghai. Thank you!” “I'll answer Xuexuan separately. Couriers travel between here and Zhejiang every day, so it's easy enough. I needn't trouble you to carry the letter.” As he spoke, He accompanied his guest out. Official propriety allowed him to go no farther than the second gate. After Hu returned to the inn, He sent four dishes for the journey, a copy of his newly printed poems and a small, heavy wooden box. On opening it, Hu found a steam pot. “How thoughtful of your master!” “My master said,” replied the attendant He Fu, “that his friendship with you is unlike any other. He told me to ask whether you need anything. If so, I'm to stay and attend to you until you've boarded your boat.” “No need. I have someone. Please go back and thank him for me.” From A’qiao's dressing case, Hu took a red envelope. There were many there, prepared for tips of varying amounts. The largest contained a five-tael banknote. He gave He Fu one of these.

Now Hu had only one thing left to do: wait for A’qiao. She had said she would arrive at noon, but the sun sank without any sign of her. Instead, Zhou returned to keep him company. “Mr Hu, I owe you so much for helping me. I've consulted someone who says His Excellency's letter carries great weight. I'm certain to get a good post.” He was smiling broadly. “Excellent!” Hu was pleased for him. “You ought to get to Yangzhou quickly. Wait too long, and the good posts will be gone.” “Never fear. There'll be stations all along the canal and both banks of the Yangtze. There are too many posts for others to snap them all up. I'll see you back to Shanghai first, then go to Yangzhou. It'll delay me ten days at most. That's nothing.” He was clearly sincere, and Hu would still need his help on the journey, so he nodded and said no more. They talked for a while. Seeing Hu restless, Zhou hesitated. Staying might annoy him, but leaving him alone at the inn would be worse. After considering, he suggested going out for a drink to take his mind off things. “Thank you, but not today. I'm waiting for someone.” “Oh—A’qiao?” Now Zhou understood his uneasiness. “Yes. She went to her parents' home in Mudu and promised to return at noon. There's still no sign of her. I don't know what's happened.” “If she isn't here now, she won't be back today. The regular passenger boat from Mudu arrived long ago.” “She didn't take the regular boat. She hired one for the return journey.” “Then I'll inquire at the Chang Gate wharves.” Zhou stood up. “How can you inquire when we don't know which boat?” “Never mind. Once I'm there, a question will tell me.” “Of course! You know everyone at the wharves. Thank you.”

Not long after Zhou left, an inn servant brought in a boy of fifteen or sixteen. He said he was a young attendant who carried messages to the inner quarters of the Pan household. Their mistress had sent him. “Please come over, Mr Hu. A lady would like to see you.” All this talk of mistresses and ladies, with the inn servant listening, embarrassed Hu. It might cause misunderstandings and gossip—always a nuisance. Instead of answering the boy, he addressed the servant. “There's another Mr Hu staying here, isn't there? He has the wrong man.” “No mistake, sir. He gave your name, Xueyan. That's why I brought him in.” “How strange.” Hu turned to the boy. “I have no friend in Suzhou called Pan, and I certainly don't know your mistress.” “It's the lady from Mudu who wants to see you. She's a close friend of our mistress.” “So it's A’qiao!” Hu was utterly puzzled. “Why did she go to your house instead of coming back to the inn?” “I don't know. She only said to ask you to come and see her.” Hu was in a quandary. How could he accept an invitation from the womenfolk of a complete stranger? Why had A’qiao gone to the Pans', and why was she asking him to meet her there? Everything raised doubts. Better not go.

Even so, he must find out what had happened. To establish whether the story was true, the first thing was to ask about A’qiao. “Have you seen this lady from Mudu?” “Yes.” “What does she look like?” The boy described her figure, features and clothes correctly. It seemed true, then, that A’qiao was at the Pan house. With that established, the next step was easy. “Very well. Wait outside, or go for a walk and come back. I must see someone I'm expecting before I can go with you.” Hu took some small change from the tea table and gave it to him. “Go and buy yourself some sweets.” “Thank you, Mr Hu. When should I come back?” “In an hour.”

Before the hour was up, the man he was waiting for returned. It was Zhou. His inquiries showed that A’qiao's boat had arrived as early as three that afternoon. “This is interesting. It seems the story is true.” Hu then told him about the unexpected invitation. “There must be a reason. A’qiao must have some difficulty about returning here. I'll go with you.” “You're right, but I don't want to go. It's the one chance in ten thousand that a man must fear.” Lowering his voice, Hu continued, “People can be treacherous. One wrong step may ruin everything. I'm always careful and try to offend no one, but I can't avoid jealousy. Someone may be plotting against me. Other matters can be explained. Anything involving the women's quarters of another household is best kept far away from. I'd like you to go for me.” Zhou had long experience of the world and had seen every kind of strange affair. Hu was afraid of an extortion trap involving a woman, he thought, and the concern was reasonable. He too must be careful if he went in Hu's place. He nodded. “I'll go. I'll simply ask A’qiao to come out and hear what she has to say.” “Exactly. Find out and come straight back to tell me.” As they spoke, the boy returned. Hu gave some convenient reason why he could not leave. The messenger could hardly object and took Zhou away.

It was some two hours before Zhou returned. “A’qiao had a great deal to say. There are things I don't fully understand.” He paused to collect his thoughts, then explained briefly. “Her husband's family sent someone who followed her here from Mudu. They seem to be looking for trouble. She didn't come back because she didn't want them to discover where she's staying. She says there are many things she must discuss with you in person. She's afraid the people following her are watching near the Pans', so she dare not leave now. She wants me to fetch her at midnight.” “Oh!” Hu was deeply surprised. “As far as I know, her husband's family are very docile. How can this be?” Zhou could offer no opinion. “You'll know when you see her.” “Wait!” Hu's eyes flashed, and his expression became stern. “You mustn't fetch her. If someone follows and accuses me tomorrow of abducting a respectable married woman, I can't afford that disgrace. Old Zhou, tell me about this Pan family.” “There are two prominent Pan families in Suzhou: the ‘Noble Pans’ and the ‘Rich Pans’. This household belongs to the same clan as the Rich Pans. A’qiao's friend is the master's concubine. His principal wife has died, so the concubine runs the household. That's why she can decide to let A’qiao stay.” “What's the master's name? Do you know?” “No.” “That doesn't matter. I'll call on him and explain what has happened. Then we can ask A’qiao to come out and talk in his presence. But this will mean asking you to accept a humble role.” Zhou understood: he was to act for the moment as a servant presenting Hu's visiting card. He did not mind and readily agreed. “I'll attend you.” They hired a sedan chair. Carrying the card case, Zhou accompanied Hu to the Pan house. When the card was brought in, the master was bewildered. His concubine understood, however, and explained. Once he grasped the situation, he immediately ordered that the visitor be received.
